Why Use Ultralytics YOLO for Inference?[#](#why-use-ultralytics-yolo-for-inference)
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Key reasons to use YOLO26's predict mode:

*   **Versatility:** Run inference on images, videos, and live streams.
*   **Performance:** Engineered for real-time, high-speed processing without sacrificing [accuracy](https://www.ultralytics.com/glossary/accuracy).
*   **Ease of Use:** Intuitive Python and CLI interfaces for rapid deployment and testing.
*   **Highly Customizable:** Various settings and parameters to tune the model's inference behavior according to your specific requirements.
*   **Production Ready:** Deploy models as [Ultralytics Platform inference endpoints](/platform/deploy/endpoints) with auto-scaling and monitoring, or run inference locally.

### Key Features of Predict Mode[#](#key-features-of-predict-mode)

YOLO26's predict mode includes:

*   **Multiple Data Source Compatibility:** Predict mode accepts individual images, collections of images, video files, and real-time video streams.
*   **Streaming Mode:** Use the streaming feature to generate a memory-efficient generator of `Results` objects. Enable this by setting `stream=True` in the predictor's call method. Unlike the default behavior (`stream=False`), which returns a list containing all results, `stream=True` yields results one at a time, making it especially useful for long videos and live streams.
*   **Batch Processing:** Process multiple images or video frames in a [single batch](https://www.ultralytics.com/blog/using-ultralytics-yolo11-to-run-batch-inferences), further reducing total inference time.
*   **Integration Friendly:** Integrate with existing data pipelines and other software components through a flexible API.

Ultralytics YOLO models return either a Python list of `Results` objects or a memory-efficient generator of `Results` objects when `stream=True` is passed to the model during inference:

Inference Arguments[#](#inference-arguments)
--------------------------------------------

`model.predict()` accepts multiple arguments that can be passed at inference time to override defaults:

### Fixed shape vs minimum rectangle (`rect`)[#](#fixed-shape-vs-minimum-rectangle-rect)

By default, predict uses **`rect=True`**, which enables **minimum-rectangle** padding when possible. The image is scaled to fit inside `imgsz` and padded only to the nearest stride multiple, so the final tensor may be **smaller** than `imgsz`. Minimum-rectangle padding is only used when **all images in the batch have the same shape** and the backend supports it (PyTorch `.pt`, or a dynamic-shape export such as dynamic ONNX). Otherwise, images are padded to the **full** `imgsz` target. Depth and RT-DETR models ignore `rect` and stretch every image to the full `imgsz` without padding.

Use **`rect=False`** to always use the full `imgsz` target. This is recommended when you need a fixed input size to match exported models (ONNX, TensorRT, etc.).

**Integer vs tuple `imgsz`**

*   An **integer** `imgsz=640` becomes a square target `(640, 640)` after stride rounding.
*   A **tuple** `imgsz=(384, 672)` sets a rectangular target. With `rect=True`, the actual tensor can be smaller than this target.

**Training vs predict/export**

Training accepts only a single integer `imgsz` (a `[h, w]` list is coerced to the largest value). Predict and export accept either an integer or a `(height, width)` tuple.

Example

PythonCLI

    from ultralytics import YOLO
    
    # Load a pretrained YOLO26n model
    model = YOLO("yolo26n.pt")
    
    # Run inference on 'bus.jpg' with arguments
    model.predict("https://ultralytics.com/images/bus.jpg", save=True, imgsz=320, conf=0.25)

Inference Devices[#](#inference-devices)
----------------------------------------

`device` takes PyTorch device names for every model format, so the same value selects the same hardware whether you run a `.pt` checkpoint or an exported model. Leave it unset to use the best available device. Each runtime maps the name onto its own hardware, and [validation](/modes/val) and [benchmarking](/modes/benchmark) take the same values:

| Format | unset | `cpu` | `0` or `cuda:0` | `mps` | `xpu` | `npu` |

| PyTorch `.pt`, [TorchScript](/integrations/torchscript) | CUDA GPU, else CPU | CPU | NVIDIA GPU | Apple GPU | Intel GPU | Huawei Ascend NPU |
| [ONNX](/integrations/onnx) | CUDA GPU, else CPU | CPU | NVIDIA GPU (CUDA), AMD GPU (MIGraphX) | Core ML | \- | \- |
| [TensorRT](/integrations/tensorrt) | NVIDIA GPU | NVIDIA GPU | NVIDIA GPU | \- | \- | \- |
| [OpenVINO](/integrations/openvino) | OpenVINO AUTO | Intel CPU | \- | \- | Intel GPU (`xpu:1` is OpenVINO `GPU.1`) | Intel NPU |
| [LiteRT](/integrations/litert) | CPU | CPU | \- | \- | Intel GPU through the OpenVINO plugin | Intel NPU through the OpenVINO plugin |
| [PaddlePaddle](/integrations/paddlepaddle) | CUDA GPU, else CPU | CPU | NVIDIA GPU | \- | \- | \- |

`-` means the runtime has no backend for that device. ONNX, TensorRT and PaddlePaddle check the name with PyTorch first, so they reject a device PyTorch cannot see and otherwise run on their default hardware. OpenVINO warns and falls back to AUTO when a requested Intel device is missing, and the LiteRT Intel plugin falls back to CPU. Other formats choose their own hardware: [CoreML](/integrations/coreml) runs on the Apple Neural Engine and CPU, [Edge TPU](/integrations/edge-tpu) takes `tpu:0`, [NCNN](/integrations/ncnn) takes `vulkan:0` for its Vulkan GPU path, and the remaining formats run on their target's CPU or accelerator. The older `intel:cpu`, `intel:gpu` and `intel:npu` names still work as deprecated aliases for `cpu`, `xpu` and `npu`.
